newsitem.title: USA: Key IMM currencies end higher, Can dlr and peso off.
newsitem.headline: Key IMM currencies end higher, Can dlr and peso off.

text.p: Key IMM currency futures ended higher, while Canadian dollar and the Mexican peso contracts weakened as the day progressed.

March Australian dollar closed slightly higher but off its daily high of $0.7818. Some hedge funds, which were long Australian dollars, liquidated those positions throughout the day, traders said. The strength in the metals markets contributed to early-morning buying in the Australian dollar futures pit, traders said.
"There has been a lot of two-way activity, but in the last hour you've seen good fund selling," one futures trader said.
They also said funds were slightly nervous holding long Canadian dollar positions in the short term.
"A lot of the funds were long Canada and got hurt over the last three weeks," he said. "They will probably re-enter and get long that market when the Canadian stabilizes."
One firm sold 1,000 March Canadian dollars late.

The peso pit, however, was bombarded with a consistent stream of sellers all day, with one firm alone dumping 2,500 of the March contracts. Banco de Mexico did not intervene despite announcing on February 19 that it would inject up to $200 million if the peso slid by more than two percent.

March pesos lost $0.002775 to end at $0.124250, after hitting a daily low of $0.123500, while the cash peso ended down 17.6 centavos in key 48-hour contracts at 7.96/7.98 per dollar -- more than two percent lower on the day.
Fears continued to mount about Mexico's drug problems, floor traders said. They are concerned about whether the U.S. will certify Mexico as an ally in its war on drugs.
In addition, dealers said U.S. dollars were flowing out of Mexico due to attractive yields on the U.S. long bond.
However, the U.S. dollar weakened slightly against the yen, Swiss francs and marks.

Some analysts said gains in marks and Swiss francs were corrections from oversold conditions on Wednesday. March marks and Swiss francs fell sharply in reaction to U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's comments that he couldn't rule out a pre-emptive tightening.
"That doesn't mean they tighten tomorrow," said David Ethridge, director of currency analysis of the Americas at MMS International.
Ethridge said long-term gains in the U.S. dollar would be built on continued structural weakness in the economies of Europe and Japan, rather than just higher U.S. rates.

At the end of pit trade, March yen were up $0.000084 at $0.008298, marks were up $0.0001 at $0.5928, Swiss francs up $0.0017 at $0.6795, sterling off $0.0094 at $1.6246, Canadian dollars were down $0.0010 at $0.7315, Australian dollars were up $0.0008 at $0.7761 and pesos were down $0.002775 at $0.124250.
